questions.q: You open a web browser to look something up. Which list puts the layers you depend on in order, from the one you use directly down to the bottom?
choices: Application -> operating system -> hardware -> physical components
Operating system -> application -> hardware -> physical components
Application -> hardware -> operating system -> physical components
Physical components -> hardware -> operating system -> application
questions.explain: You run an application written by other programmers, for an OS written by other developers, running on hardware produced by other manufacturers, made of physical components like metal, rubber, plastic, and electricity.

questions.q: When you use the Calculator app, which layer sits directly beneath the application?
questions.explain: Applications are written for an operating system, and the OS in turn runs on the hardware.

questions.q: In the layered view of everyday computer use, what does the operating system run on?
questions.explain: The OS runs on hardware produced by other manufacturers. Applications are written for the OS.

questions.q: Which of these are given as examples of the physical components that hardware is made of?
questions.explain: The bottom layer is physical: metal, rubber, plastic, electricity, etc. Protocols and OS code are not physical materials.

questions.q: What does it mean to say we usually interact with a computer at a "superficial level"?
choices: We use it mostly for unimportant tasks such as games
We work through layers (applications, OS, hardware) built by other people without dealing with what lies beneath them
We only touch the outside of the machine, such as the keyboard and screen
We use it without connecting to a network
questions.explain: Browsing, file navigation, calculation, and games all happen through an application, for an OS, on hardware, made of physical components, each built by someone else. We stay on the surface of that stack.

questions.q: Writing a program in a high-level language such as Python or C++ means you are interacting with the machine directly at the hardware level.
questions.explain: Even high-level programming is still superficial: the editor/IDE is (probably) someone else's application, and the language was (probably) developed by someone else and exists in a human-readable form.

questions.q: Why is programming in a high-level language still considered a superficial way of interacting with the machine?
choices: The text editor or IDE is (probably) an application someone else developed
The language itself was (probably) developed by someone else
The language exists in a human-readable form
Programs written in C++ never actually run on hardware
questions.explain: The tools and the language are layers built by others, and the code is human-readable text, not what the machine itself works with. High-level programs can do arithmetic and do run on hardware, through those layers.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: a high-level programming language like Python or C++ exists in a ______-readable form.
questions.explain: High-level languages are written in a human-readable form. That is one reason programming in them is still a layer above the machine.

questions.q: Surfing the Internet, navigating file systems with File Explorer, and using the Calculator all involve running an application someone else wrote.
questions.explain: Each everyday task is done by running an application (browser, File Explorer, Calculator, a game) written by other programmers.

questions.q: What is the best answer to the question "What is a computer?"
choices: Any electronic device that performs calculations
There is no perfect definition of a computer
A machine that runs an operating system
A device that contains hardware, software, data, and protocols
questions.explain: There is no perfect definition of a computer. Modern computers tend to share five characteristics, but those are typical traits, not a strict definition.

questions.q: What did the word "computer" originally refer to?
questions.explain: "Computer" was originally a job. People were hired as "computers" to perform numerous or complex calculations.

questions.q: Which organizations hired human "computers"?
questions.explain: Governments, research labs, and large companies hired "computers" to do numerous or complex calculations.

questions.q: Human "computers" performed numerous or complex calculations by hand or with simple tools.
questions.explain: That was the original job: calculations done by hand or with simple tools.

questions.q: Which of these are among the characteristics that computers in the modern sense tend to have?
questions.explain: The five characteristics are: operate automatically; perform arithmetic/logical operations; store, process, and retrieve data; programmable; electronic. Network connections and displays are not on the list.

questions.q: Which devices arguably function as computers, even though we generally wouldn't call them computers?
questions.explain: Mechanical cash registers and player pianos are the gray-area examples. They have some computer-like traits but not all of them.

questions.q: A mechanical cash register adds up totals, and a player piano plays by itself from a music roll. Which modern-computer characteristic do BOTH clearly lack?
choices: Neither lacks any of the five characteristics
questions.explain: Both are mechanical, not electronic. The cash register does arithmetic, and the player piano operates automatically, so each has some traits. That is why they only 'arguably' count as computers.

questions.q: The five characteristics of a modern computer form a strict test: a device lacking any one of them cannot be considered a computer.
questions.explain: Modern computers 'tend to have' these characteristics. They are typical traits, not a strict test, which is consistent with there being no perfect definition of a computer.

questions.q: Name the modern-computer characteristic that means the machine can be given new instructions to change what it does.
questions.explain: Programmable is one of the five characteristics, along with operating automatically, performing arithmetic/logical operations, storing/processing/retrieving data, and being electronic.

questions.q: What is a computer system?
choices: A computer that is connected to a network
The operating system that runs a computer
The set of components that work together to enable a computing device (a computer) to function
The physical hardware inside a computer's case
questions.explain: A computer system is the set of components (hardware, software, data, protocols) that work together to let a computer function.

questions.q: Which of these are components of a computer system?
questions.explain: The four components are hardware, software, data, and protocols. Electricity is a physical material that hardware is made of, not a separate component.

questions.q: "Computer" and "computer system" mean the same thing.
questions.explain: The computer is the device. The computer system is the set of components (hardware, software, data, protocols) that work together so the device can function.

questions.q: Which computer system component is defined as "the material components of the system"?
questions.explain: Hardware is the material components of the system, such as the CPU, memory, disks, and keyboard.

questions.q: Which component is defined as "the set of instructions that tell the hardware what to do"?
questions.explain: Software is defined by its job: the instructions that tell the hardware what to do.

questions.q: Which component is defined as "information (and its physical form) present in the system"?
questions.explain: Data is information together with its physical form in the system.

questions.q: Which component is defined as "standards and procedures applied to computers"?
questions.explain: Protocols are the standards and procedures applied to computers, such as the rules machines follow to exchange messages over a network.

questions.q: By definition, data includes both the information itself and its physical form in the system.
questions.explain: Data is information (and its physical form) present in the system. Leaving out the physical form is a common mistake.

questions.q: Two computers follow an agreed set of rules for exchanging messages over a network. Which computer system component are those rules?
questions.explain: Agreed rules for how machines communicate are standards and procedures applied to computers, which makes them protocols.

questions.q: Which classification is correct?
questions.explain: A saved photo is information stored in the system, so it is data. A web browser and an OS are software (instructions), and RAM chips are hardware (material components).

questions.q: An operating system is an example of software.
questions.explain: An OS is a set of instructions that tell the hardware what to do, so it is software.

questions.q: In computer systems and networks, virtually no statement is both useful and categorically true; there is almost always an exception.
questions.explain: Useful general statements about systems usually describe the typical case. Expect exceptions.

questions.q: Once a fact about computer systems is established, you can count on it staying true as technology advances.
questions.explain: Technology is advancing and changing all the time. What is true today may not be true tomorrow.

questions.q: A reference states that "computers are electronic." Given how general statements about systems should be read, what is the best interpretation?
choices: It is a categorical rule with no exceptions
It is true in general or in the typical case, and exceptions may exist
It is false, because exceptions exist
It applies only to historical computers
questions.explain: Virtually no useful statement in systems is categorically true. Being electronic is something modern computers tend to have, not an absolute rule.

questions.q: In the statement "computers in the modern sense tend to have the following characteristics," which words show that the list describes typical traits rather than an absolute requirement?
questions.explain: "Tend to have" means these are usual traits, not strict requirements. That matches the idea that there is no perfect definition of a computer.

questions.q: That mechanical cash registers and player pianos "arguably" function as computers shows that the boundary of what counts as a computer is fuzzy rather than sharp.
questions.explain: These gray-area devices have some computer traits but not all of them. That is why there is no perfect definition and why general statements have exceptions.
